en: Sutta Nipāta 2.7 Brāhmaṇadhammikasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then a number of wealthy Kosalan brahmins—aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life—approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those wealthy brahmins said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, do the brahmins of today conform to the brahminical dharma of the ancient brahmins?
“Brahmin, the brahmins of today do not conform to the brahminical dharma of the ancient brahmins.
“It would be well, Master Gotama, if you would speak to us about the brahminical dharma of the ancient brahmins, if it is not too much trouble for you.”
“In that case, brahmins, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” those wealthy brahmins replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In former times there were seers,
self-restrained and practicing austerities;
having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, they lived.”
They wandered about seeking their own welfare.
There were no cattle for the brahmins,
nor gold, nor grain-stores.
They possessed the wealth of recitation and were the guardians of the Brahmā-treasure;
whatever they had prepared, [they offered].
The door-portion was set out;
they thought that it should be given to those who inspire faith and are seekers.
With garments of various colors,
beds, and dwellings;
with flourishing provinces and kingdoms.
They paid homage to the brahmins.
The brahmins were not to be slain,
invincible, and protected by the Dhamma.
No one at all prevented him from entering the doors of families in every way.
For forty-eight years, he remained thus.
In former times, those brahmins lived the celibate life from their youth; they practiced the pursuit of true knowledge and conduct.
The Brahmins did not go to another [woman],
nor did they buy a wife;
they lived together only through mutual affection.
Having come together, they resolved upon battle,
except for that occasion regarding the abstention from violence.
The brahmins do not engage in sexual intercourse even in private;
they maintain both the holy life and virtuous conduct.
They praised straightforwardness, gentleness, austerity, amiability,
non-violence, and patience.
He who was their supreme leader,
Brahmā of firm resolve,
even he [engaged] in the practice of sexual intercourse.
Even in his dreams he did not come.
Some here of wise nature, training themselves in his practice, [followed him].
They praised the holy life,
virtuous conduct, and patience;
[they praised] rice, bedding, and clothing.
Having requested ghee and oil,
and having gathered them together in accordance with the Dhamma,
they then prepared the sacrifice.
While the sacrifice was being performed,
they did not slaughter those cows,
just as one would not harm a mother, a father, or a brother.
And other kinsmen as well;
cows are our supreme friends,
from whom medicinal herbs are born.
She is the giver of food, the giver of strength,
the giver of beauty, and likewise the giver of happiness;
having understood this essential meaning, [one should honor her].
May no cattle harm you—
those who are delicate-limbed, large-bodied,
beautiful, and renowned.
As long as brahmins, diligent in what ought and ought not to be done, persisted in their own duties within the world, so long did they endure.
This generation has grown accustomed to pleasure.
Having seen [the world] down to its subtlest atom, they have fallen into perversion.
And the women, beautifully adorned, gave their response to the king as he stood by the chariot yoked with thoroughbred steeds.
In the cutting of cloth, in weaving,
in a dwelling, and in a settlement,
it is divided and measured into portions.
Surrounded by a circle of attendants and accompanied by a multitude of excellent women,
he enjoyed sublime human pleasures.
The brahmins became covetous;
having composed mantras there,
they approached Okkāka.
You possess abundant wealth and grain;
sacrifice, for you have much riches;
sacrifice, for you have much wealth.
Then the king, that bull among chariot-warriors,
being entreated by the brahmins,
[prepared for] the horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice.
Having performed the Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, and the Niraggaḷa sacrifices,
he gave wealth to the brahmins.
Cows, a bed, and clothing;
women well-adorned;
and chariots yoked with thoroughbred steeds—
In the well-wrought weaving of the mind,
there are delightful dwellings,
beautifully divided into their respective parts.
Having filled [the vessels] with various kinds of grain,
he gave wealth to the brahmins.
And they, having received that wealth there,
They took delight in hoarding;
for those who were overwhelmed by desire,
craving increased all the more.
Having composed mantras there,
they returned once more to Okkāka.
Just as water and earth...
Gold is wealth and property;
likewise, cattle are the equipment for human beings,
for they are the requisites of living creatures.
Sacrifice; you have much wealth, sacrifice; you have much treasure.
Then the king was thus exhorted.
The bull among chariot-warriors had many hundreds of thousands of cows slaughtered in sacrifice by the brahmins.
Neither with their feet nor with their horns do they harm anyone by any means;
cows are like rams.
The soratā cows that yield milk in jars—
the king, having seized them by their horns, had them slaughtered with a sword.
Then the gods, the ancestors, Indra, the asuras,
and the rakkhasas cried out, "Injustice!"
Whatever weapon falls upon living beings,
there were three diseases in former times:
desire, hunger, and old age.
From the slaughter of animals,
ninety-eight [offenses] were incurred;
this is the unrighteousness of punishments.
The old order has passed away;
those who do no harm are slain,
and the religious duties of the sacrificers fall into ruin.
Thus is this minor rule,
ancient and censured by the wise;
wherever one sees such a thing, [one should avoid it].
People revile the officiating priest.
When the Dhamma has thus fallen into disorder,
the Suddas and Vessikas are split apart.
The Kṣatriyas were divided and at variance;
they treated their husbands with contempt as if they were wives.
Both the Kṣatriyas and those who claimed to be kinsmen of Brahmā—
And others who are protected by their clan,
having rejected talk of birth,
have come under the sway of sensual pleasures.
When this was said, those wealthy brahmins said to the Blessed One:
"Magnificent, Master Gotama! ... [as before] ...
May Master Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts."
The Seventh Discourse on the Duties of a Brahmin.
